demo_heboss.summary: Mr. He is a results-driven boss with a fast pace. He watches costs and payments very closely, but he also gives resources and credits good work. You two work together smoothly right now and he trusts you, but several things lately are tight on timing, so you need to push things forward proactively and sync up in time, and not let him feel you're slow.

points.text: Impatient, wants results without waiting for process: on Saturday he spotted a low profit margin and wanted a rough estimate the same day, refusing to wait until next week.
Sensitive about money, keeps a close eye on costs, payments, and budgets, but isn't just about cutting corners—he cares about value for money.
Has a strong sense of milestones; once a time is set he wants to see something, and he doesn't like sloppy work.
Willing to give space to reliable people; when hiring he stressed that people need to be reliable and salary is negotiable, which shows he values ability over driving down pay.
Project profit and cost control—he can't sit still when the profit margin drops.
Payment milestones; he explicitly asked to keep an eye on the first payment.
Client relationships and speed of progress; he warned not to let the other side feel things are slow again.
Balancing occasion and value for money; the annual party should be lively but not over budget.
The team being presentable and able to show up well; the performance needs to be stage-worthy, no slacking.
He trusts you, handing you key client contact and contract progress, and praised you to your face after the contract was signed.
He dangles carrots but also gives real signals, mentioning the year-end bonus is secured.
He expects delivery from you, having you lead meetings and including you in design and development, which shows he sees you as the project lead.
When something is urgent to him, give a rough estimate or progress snapshot first—don't wait for perfection, he fears waiting more.
Proactively sync payment and client updates, especially that payment at month-end; keep on it and let him know you're on it.
For things like the annual party and performances, give options and budget comparisons in advance, highlight value for money, and don't just quote high prices.
When recommending people, spell out why they're reliable; you can be bold about salary, since he clearly said it's negotiable.
Before the meeting next Monday, get the redesign progress and the Mr. Wang situation straight, align design and development in advance, and don't get caught off guard in the meeting.

demo_zhoujie.summary: Ms. Zhou is your direct supervisor. She's organized and puts risk first, pushes her team but also supports them, and will fight for resources for you and back you up in reviews. You two have good trust right now, and she's willing to hand you the main presentation and mentoring newcomers. Lately, note this: her schedule is packed and she often works weekends, so when you report, state risks and testing time realistically and tell her early—don't let her find out last; also, she keeps reminding you not to stay up late, so don't push yourself too hard.

points.text: Methodical, likes to set the rhythm clearly: weekly report format, schedule milestones, and handover arrangements are all agreed in advance.
Strong risk awareness; she'd rather hear bad news early than be blindsided at the end.
Highly dedicated, often revising plans and pushing progress on weekends and holidays, with a very full schedule.
Protective of her team, willing to back them up in front of clients and to fight for resources for the team.
She wants stability and dislikes sudden changes. Before a demo, she'll remind you to slow down and not change anything.
She pushes hard, but also keeps telling you to rest — not the type who only squeezes people dry.
She cares about progress transparency: a short update every Friday covering what you did, what's blocked, and next week's plan.
She wants risks surfaced early. Things like an API not being connected must be reported honestly, not hidden until the end.
She cares about complete schedules and specifically reminds you to include testing time — don't leave it out again.
She cares about delivery quality. Review feedback gets compiled into a doc and must be addressed within a deadline.
She cares about the team's well-being and reminds you not to carry everything alone or stay up late rushing.
She cares about her own promises — she'll push for raises and headcount, and she'll keep you posted on progress.
She trusts you, handing you the lead presenter role for the client review and saying clearly she'll back you up.
She recognizes your output, praised your weekly report format and review performance, and wants you to keep using that format.
She's willing to give you room to grow, agreeing to let Lin handle a module independently — with you covering if problems come up.
When you're on leave, she'll step in to look after the new hire — day-to-day coordination is smooth.
Overall it's a mentor-style trust within a boss-subordinate relationship: she piles on responsibility but also gives support, and you can handle it.
Keep weekly reports short and factual, don't sugarcoat risks, and send them on time every Friday.
Proactively include testing time in schedules — don't wait for her to remind you.
Report changes or blockers as early as possible; don't drag it to the last minute.
When she tells you not to stay up late, don't just say yes — let her see you're actually adjusting your pace.
She's busy on weekends too, so save non-urgent matters for weekdays; for urgent ones, just explain clearly.
No need to keep pushing on the raise and headcount she promised to fight for — doing the project well is the best follow-up.

demo_daliu.summary: Da Liu is a reliable, responsible colleague. His second child is due soon, so family is taking a lot of his energy, and he's especially sensitive to changing requirements and last-minute add-ons. You work well together and he's willing to take things on, but lately you should help lock down requirements, minimize changes, and not bother him during his leave.

points.text: He's solid and dependable — if he promises something, he'll find a way to finish it, even if it means weekend overtime.
He has good technical judgment and flags risks early — like the login page white-screen risk, which he noted and scheduled for phase two.
He doesn't like being the main presenter in front of clients; he'd rather just handle technical questions and hopes not to be pushed into the spotlight during demos.
He's deeply committed to family — he leaves early to care for his wife when she's unwell during pregnancy, and often spends weekends caring for the kid, cooking, and looking after her.
He hates changing requirements and "estimates turning into commitments," and will say so directly, asking to cut scope before scheduling.
He cares about schedule stability and doesn't want requirements changing daily — repeated additions make him feel estimates become commitments.
He cares about actually resting during leave and said clearly: no calls during his two weeks of paternity leave, and he won't handle other modules either.
He cares about his wife and kid — her pregnancy discomfort, checkups, cooking, and childcare all come first.
He cares about delivery quality — low-probability but serious issues like the login white screen get noted and scheduled for phase two.
He cares about wrapping up the schedule early and wants features that should ship before his leave to go out — he'll proactively ask to pull together a must-do list.
Cooperation is smooth and he's open with you — like sounding you out early about paternity leave and explaining his family situation.
He'll take on requirements you raise but sets clear scheduling boundaries — e.g., the red-dot feature can't fit this week, so next week.
You have a small mutual-understanding thing going: you bought him milk tea over the requirement churn and he remembers it; he worked overtime fixing bugs and you cooperated.
During his leave, the login module is handed over to Xiao Chen — don't bypass the handover to reach him directly.
Lock requirements down in one go where possible; avoid last-minute add-ons. If you must add, first discuss what to cut and push the schedule back — don't have him estimate first.
Confirm roles in advance for demos — let him handle only technical questions, don't push him to present on the spot.
Don't call him during his two-week leave; go through Xiao Chen for login module matters.
Before his leave, pull together a clear must-do list, help him wrap up the schedule early, and cut what needs cutting early.
He has a lot going on at home — be flexible when he occasionally leaves early or catches up on weekends; don't be too rigid on timing.
The login white-screen issue is scheduled for phase two and the client approved the plan — stop bringing it up repeatedly and just follow the plan.

demo_xiaolin.summary: Lin is a conscientious, sensitive colleague who has high standards for her work but is worn down lately by constantly changing requirements and having credit taken. She's quietly looking at outside opportunities. You're close — she trusts you, relies on your feedback and support, but is also sensitive to you being vague or late. What to watch lately: keep her job hunt secret, give her specific and clear responses, and don't let the points mall work get dumped on her again.

points.text: She's diligent with high standards for herself — she'll revise her portfolio repeatedly until satisfied before submitting.
She tends to get anxious and nervous early — before reviews and interviews she'll repeatedly confirm things and practice her self-introduction, even getting so nervous her legs go weak.
She expresses emotions directly — when tired she'll say "I'm falling apart" or "I can't take it," and she'll call out dissatisfaction to your face.
She has a self-deprecating streak and will ask "do you think I'm bad at this?" — she needs affirmation from others.
In daily life she loves cats and milk tea, likes going out on weekends, and doesn't like being alone much.
She cares about her efforts being seen and really resents credit being taken by Zhang Jie or the team lead.
She cares about attribution — repeatedly asking that her name not be on the membership center submission before approval, and that no non-contributors be added to the mall project.
She cares whether people's words count — she's sensitive to vague phrases like "I'll try" and to lateness.
She cares that the job hunt stays private — repeatedly stressing secrecy and specifically checking whether you've told anyone.
She cares about work pace and health — she'll remind you to drink less cold stuff, though she herself often stays up till one or two.
She treats you as someone she can entrust secrets to — job hunting, interviews, portfolio — she only tells you in detail.
She relies on your feedback — she asks you to review her portfolio logic and pitch, and she'll revise based on what you say.
You're also actually helping her carry things — you offered to cover the points mall and to talk to Zhang Jie for her.
You meet up quite often privately — exhibitions, markets, hotpot, going to her place to pet her cat — closer than ordinary colleagues.
She has some small complaints about you but says them directly — like you always say "whatever" or "I'll try," and being late — which shows she still cares about this relationship.
Keep the job hunt and interviews strictly confidential — she's checked with you repeatedly, so don't breathe a word in the team.
Try to be specific in your answers — stop saying things like "whatever" or "I'll try." She's said clearly she wants concrete opinions and some reassurance from you.
Try not to be late for agreed times — she's already called you out on punctuality once.
Before the points mall work started, she specifically asked you not to dump it on her again — you promised to cover it, so remember to follow through.
When she's nervous or anxious, give her specific reassurance rather than vague comfort—she worries about things like "do you think I'm bad at this."
She reminded me to return the power bank and keyboard. I already said the keyboard is a gift to her, so remember to bring the power bank.

demo_amy.summary: Amy is a client who works hard to juggle a strong-willed boss and vendors, and she'll step in to shield you from some last-minute requests. She follows through on things but often gets held up by headquarters processes and her boss's sudden whims. You two are coordinating smoothly right now—she trusts you and is willing to take your advice, so it's a collaborative relationship. Things to watch lately: her boss's requirements on brand tone and the homepage direction are repetitive and unclear, and she's under a lot of pressure. When you give her proposals, try to leave her room to explain things so she doesn't get put on the spot in meetings.

points.text: When her boss adds last-minute requests, she won't just dump them on you—she'll confirm things herself first before having you start.
She reflects on how she communicates with her boss and tends to avoid direct confrontation, preferring to guide things slowly rather than push back head-on.
She's fairly sensitive to budget and work hours, and when she knows the dev workload will increase she'll pull back on her own rather than force it.
When she's caught in the middle she'll openly say she's tired and in a tough spot, but she won't shift blame—she'll apologize and say she's done her best.
She's good about following through—she'll double-check the final brand manual to make sure it's correct, and on details she's willing to have design produce variants to accommodate.
She's still at the office on the weekend catching up on weekly reports, which shows she really cares about her boss's reporting habits and is willing to put in extra time to get the details right.
She cares about her boss's views on brand tone and details—when her boss says she can't quite grasp it, she takes it to heart and it upsets her.
She cares about budget and resource boundaries and doesn't want things to spiral out of control because of added scope.
She cares about the rhythm of working with you—she'll tell you in advance "don't rush to do it," and she'll agree to note down added scope and flag it early.
She cares about keeping the launch messaging safe—she took your advice to report a conservative timeline, which shows she doesn't want to overpromise in front of her boss.
She cares about how things look at her boss's morning meeting—the weekly report gets read aloud and her boss likes details, so she'll work overtime on weekends for it.
She treats you as someone she can talk things over with—when her boss suddenly added a lottery entry, she told you not to rush into it and went to confirm herself.
She'll apologize to you and say she's "done her best," which shows she cares what you think of her and doesn't want you to feel she isn't helping.
You gave her a countdown add-on and she agreed to note it down and flag it early—there's give and take on both sides, so coordination is smooth.
She'll take your advice and adjust how she reports things, which shows she trusts your judgment.
Overall it's a collaborative relationship—she leans toward execution and coordination, you lean toward proposals and delivery, and you cover for each other.
When her boss adds last-minute requests, wait for her to confirm before acting—don't just do it directly, so she can explain it to her boss.
Spell out added scope and work hours in advance—her budget is tight, so she'll decide for herself whether to do it; don't add it after the fact.
When she's feeling stuck in the middle, give her fewer lectures and more actionable options—like cutting scope or clearly marking interactions—to ease the pressure of being questioned in meetings.
When her boss can't articulate the brand tone, include an extra variant or annotations in your proposal so she has something to explain.
Keep helping her report launch timelines conservatively—she wants to be cautious anyway, and if you give her reasons she'll take them.
She's still catching up on weekly reports on the weekend, so try not to push non-urgent things onto the weekend—leave her room to deal with her boss's sudden whims.

demo_wangzong.summary: Mr. Wang is a pragmatic client who cares about details and how things are reported, and he has a clear desire to control the project direction while also being heavily influenced by his own boss. You're currently at a key point with phase-one acceptance and phase-two kickoff, and the relationship is professional and smooth. Things to watch lately: go to tomorrow's meeting alone, talk direction first without quoting prices, make the fonts in materials bigger, keep the demo short and formal, and focus on preparing the membership system content.

points.text: He's methodical and sets communication boundaries and pace in advance—like asking you to go alone and to talk direction first without rushing to quote.
He's sensitive to details, especially user-experience things like loading speed and button feedback—he's afraid of lag at launch.
His taste leans steady and conservative—he doesn't like flashy or overly heavy visual elements, and he's thinking about people his age.
He cares about how things come across to his boss and will adjust materials (like making fonts bigger) and the demo pace to fit his boss's habits.
In decisions he'll factor in his boss's opinions but also give his own approval and adjustments along the way—he's not purely passive.
He cares whether the project direction is clear and wants to align on direction before discussing price, to avoid getting into business details too early.
He cares about his boss's experience and patience—asking for bigger fonts and a short demo shows he values smooth upward reporting.
He cares about budget control and said clearly to use the saved time to refine things—features can be cut but the budget can't be exceeded.
He cares about stability and smoothness after launch, and specifically mentioned loading speed and button feedback.
He cares about the membership system as a key point—when discussing phase-two direction he specifically asked to focus on it.
Right now phase-one acceptance and phase-two kickoff are running in parallel, the collaboration proceeds per contract, and the final payment of 140k is due after acceptance.
Mr. Wang trusts you fairly well—he'll message you directly past nine at night to add requests, and he approved of the draft you turned around quickly.
In communication he prefers to talk direction in person, which shows he values face-to-face communication—the relationship is professional but has a bit of personal rapport.
His boss is also interested in phase two and wants to talk in person, which means tomorrow's meeting might not be just Mr. Wang—be ready to face a higher level.
Tomorrow go alone as he asked, talk phase-two direction first, focus on preparing the membership system, don't proactively quote, and don't overstate the numbers.
Bring the printed checklist and a copy of the contract, make the checklist fonts bigger, keep the demo within fifteen minutes, and dress formally.
When discussing phase two, explain the membership system clearly while leaving room for budget control—emphasize using the saved time to refine things.
On details, proactively bring up optimizing loading speed and button feedback to show you care about stability—this will put him at ease.
If the boss is present, keep the demo short, speak at a moderate pace, use bigger fonts in materials, and don't let the boss lose patience.
